Gasparo Contarini
gäs-pä´rō kŏn-tä-rē´nē
n. (Gasparo Contarini, 1483–1542, Venetian statesman and cardinal, leader of the Catholic reform party, who agreed a formula of double justification with the Protestants at Regensburg in 1541)
Italian Contarini, an ancient Venetian patrician house; Gasparo, from the traditional name of one of the magi.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gasparo Contarini is the most attractive figure on the Roman side of the age. A Venetian diplomat raised to the cardinalate as a layman, he had undergone in 1511 an experience he described in terms a Protestant would recognize: that no satisfaction of his own could stand before God, and that he must rest on the righteousness of Christ. He led the commission whose Consilium de Emendanda Ecclesia of 1537 catalogued the curia's abuses so frankly that it was placed on the Index. At the Colloquy of Regensburg in 1541 he and Melanchthon and Bucer agreed on an article of justification by faith in which the believer is accepted for the imputed righteousness of Christ while an inherent righteousness follows — the formula called double justification. Rome repudiated it; so did Luther and Calvin. The texts the Reformers held against it are decisive: Rom 4:6 speaks of the man “unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,” and Php 3:9 of being found in Him “not having mine own righteousness.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines imputation as the act of imputing or charging; attribution; and to impute, in theology, as to charge or attribute to one what belongs to another.

expand to see more

IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; generally in an ill sense.

2. In theology, the act of attributing to one what properly belongs to another; as the imputation of Christ's righteousness to believers.

IMPU'TE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of.

Key Scripture

Rom 4:6 — "Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,"

Php 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

Rom 10:3 — "For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God."

Gal 5:4 — "Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace."

Modern Corruption

Double justification was an honest attempt to say both things at once, and it failed because justification will not share its ground with anything inherent.

expand to see more

The Regensburg formula tried to hold that the believer is accepted on account of Christ's imputed righteousness and also that a righteousness wrought within him belongs to his justification. The Reformers saw that the second clause destroys the first, because a ground that is partly inherent is not grace but a mixture, and the conscience can never know how much of its own is required. Rom 10:3 names the failure precisely: men “going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.” Gal 5:4 is blunter: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law.”

The modern corruption is the ecumenical revival of the same device, in documents that declare the sixteenth-century condemnations no longer to apply while leaving the Tridentine canons in force. Contarini's attempt deserves more respect than its descendants, because he genuinely believed both halves and was trying to state a conversion he had actually had. But the distinction that must be kept is the one the Reformation made and never conceded: sanctification is real, inward and necessary, and it is the fruit of justification, never a part of its ground. Rom 4:6 gives the ground, “without works.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logizomai (G3049), to impute, to reckon; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; hupotasso (G5293), to submit.

expand to see more

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to impute; Romans 4:6.

Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; Romans 4:6, Philippians 3:9.

Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to submit, to subject oneself; Romans 10:3.

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to make of no effect; Galatians 5:4.

Greek ekpipto (G1601) — to fall out of, to fall from; Galatians 5:4.

Usage

"“unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6) — the ground that admits no addition."

"“not having mine own righteousness” (Php 3:9) — against an inherent ground."

"“going about to establish their own righteousness” (Rom 10:3) — the failure named."
